title: Wait for all your mail
allegory: Backprop is a mailroom where the loss writes feedback to everyone who helped make it, and a topological sort is the writing schedule: nobody sends their own letters until every letter owed to them has arrived.
map: a node (tensor) in the computational graph
edges from a value to the operations that consumed it
one gradient contribution sent back along an edge
waiting until every letter owed to you has arrived
visiting a node only after all its consumers have contributed
the writing schedule pinned on the wall
the topological order: loss first, parameters last
credit: The 'every edge points one way' picture of a topological sort follows Andrej Karpathy's micrograd lecture (The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation).

chapters.name: Who writes first?
chapters.note: every node passes its feedback on once. In what order?

cap.1: Backprop hands feedback from the loss back to every value that helped make it. Each value passes its feedback on exactly once. So who goes first matters.
cap.2: Backprop walks the computational graph from the loss backwards, calling each node's backward once. Call a node too early and it passes on an incomplete gradient.
cap.3: Reverse-mode AD fires each node's backward exactly once, so its grad_out must be complete when it fires. That is an ordering constraint over the whole DAG.

cap.1: Picture a mailroom. The loss writes feedback to whoever helped make it. Each helper waits until every letter owed to them has arrived, then writes their own.
cap.2: Each node is a helper and each edge an 'I used your work' link. b fed both c and d, so b waits for letters from both before it writes to a.
cap.3: Letters are gradient contributions along edges and the inbox is the accumulated grad. A node may fire only after all of its consumers have fired.

cap.1: Why wait? Because b's full feedback is the sum of every letter it gets. Send yours on after one letter and you pass on half the story.
cap.2: b fed two consumers, so dL/db is the gradient arriving via c plus the gradient arriving via d. The total only exists once both have arrived.
cap.3: Multivariate chain rule: ∂L/∂b = Σᵤ ∂L/∂u · ∂u/∂b over consumers u. A node's grad is a sum over its out-edges; that sum is why the order constraint exists.

cap.1: Pin up a schedule where every helper comes after everyone who used their work: L, then c and d, then b, then a. Every arrow points the same way.
cap.2: A topological sort lines the graph up so every edge points one way. Walked from the loss, each node runs after all its consumers. c and d may go in either order.
cap.3: Any linear extension of the DAG's partial order works. Ties like (c, d) are free because accumulation commutes. A valid order exists only if the graph has no cycle.

chapters.name: Suppliers first
chapters.title: the list depth-first search builds (walk it right to left)

cap.1: To build the schedule, start at the loss and chase suppliers first. Write a helper down only once all its suppliers are written, then read the list backwards.
cap.2: Depth-first search from the loss: recurse into each node's inputs, append the node once they are done, skip anything already visited. Reverse the list to backprop.
cap.3: Post-order DFS over get_children puts leaves before the root; reversed, it is a valid backward order. Meeting a node that is still in progress means a cycle: raise.

chapters.name: The early letter

left.title: in topological order
lines: b waits for c and d
sends the full sum to a

chapters.verdict: A wrong order gives wrong gradients, not a crash.

cap.1: Let b write after only c's letter and d's letter lands on an empty desk. a gets half the feedback. Nothing crashes; training just quietly gets worse.
cap.2: Visit a tensor before all its consumers contribute and it back-propagates a partial gradient: no exception, plausible numbers. That is why [0.4] has you write the sort yourself.
cap.3: An order violation fires backward with an incomplete grad_out. The result is well-shaped and roughly aligned, so only a check against a reference (PyTorch, central differences) exposes it.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: loss.backward() does this sort for you
Trust the gradients you read later

cap.1: You will rarely write this sort again: loss.backward() does it. Knowing why the order matters is how you trust every gradient you read later.
cap.2: PyTorch's autograd does the ordering for you; this is the one time you open the box. Same pattern anywhere work depends on other work: builds, installs, spreadsheets.
cap.3: Gradient-based tools you will meet for understanding and steering models ride this same backward walk; a correct order is what makes those numbers trustworthy.

coda.title: Rows are helpers L, c, d, b, a (top to bottom); columns are time slots 1 to 5. Fix the schedule.

caption.1: This schedule lets b write too early, so a gets 6 instead of 21. Move the lights until the late-letter list is empty and a gets its full 21.
caption.2: Each lit cell says when a node runs backward. Every node must run after everyone who used it. Try putting c and d in the same slot: ties are fine.
caption.3: Forward: b = 3a, c = 2b, d = 5b, L = c + d, so dL/da = 21. Firing b before d drops the 5·3 = 15 term along that path: a partial gradient, silently.

hamming.what: A line-up of a graph's nodes in which no node is visited before everything that depends on it.
hamming.when: Whenever work flows through a graph of dependencies; in ML it happens inside loss.backward() every step, and you write it by hand once in [0.4].
hamming.why: Backprop gives each node one chance to pass its gradient on, and that gradient is a sum over its consumers, so it must be complete before the node fires.

object.title: The mail tower
object.subtitle: The graph stood on end: the loss at the top, every letter falling downhill to the parameter at the bottom.

cap.1: Stand the graph on end with the loss on top. Every letter now falls downhill: nothing ever has to travel back up.
cap.2: Height is schedule position. Every edge points down, which is exactly what a topological order means.
cap.3: Embedding a DAG by topological rank makes every edge monotone in height; that is the order's defining property.

cap.1: From above it looks like a tangle. From the side the order is plain: top floor first, bottom floor last.
cap.2: The same graph viewed flat hides the order; the sort is what recovers it.
cap.3: A topological order is a projection of the DAG onto a line that preserves every edge's direction.

cap.1: c and d share a floor. Neither used the other's work, so either can write first.
cap.2: Ties are free: nodes with no path between them can run in any order.
cap.3: c and d are incomparable in the partial order; accumulation commutes, so any interleaving gives identical gradients.

cap.1: b's inbox takes two letters, one from each floor above. b writes only once both have landed.
cap.2: Fan-out in the forward pass means fan-in on the way back: b's gradient is the sum of both letters.
cap.3: In-degree 2 in the backward graph: ∂L/∂b = ∂L/∂c·∂c/∂b + ∂L/∂d·∂d/∂b, complete only after both consumers fire.

predict.q: b was used by both c and d. When can b run its backward?

options.t: Only after both c and d have run
As soon as either one has run

predict.why: b's gradient is the sum of the letters from c and d. Fire after one and you pass on half.

predict.q: c and d each feed only L. Does it matter which goes first?

options.t: Yes, c must always go first

predict.why: Neither depends on the other, and gradient contributions add, which works in any order.

predict.q: By mistake, b runs before d. What happens?

options.t: Smaller, wrong gradients and no error
An immediate crash with a shape error

predict.why: A partial gradient has the right shape and a plausible direction, so nothing complains. Training just gets quietly worse.
